gaps.sentence: ___ John and his brother are doctors.
gaps.explanation: 'Both John and his brother are ...' links two people affirmatively; 'neither' and 'either' pair with 'nor/or'.

gaps.sentence: Don't rush — we've got ___ of time.
gaps.hint: fixed pattern: ___ of time (no article needed)
gaps.explanation: 'Plenty of time' needs no article; 'lot of time' would need 'a', and 'much of time' needs 'the'.

gaps.sentence: Three out of four respondents — that is, the ___ — supported the change.
gaps.hint: three out of four = more than half
gaps.explanation: Three out of four is more than half, so 'the majority' is the correct label.

gaps.sentence: ___ of the two films has been shown on television.
gaps.explanation: 'Neither of the two films has ...' is correct for two items; 'none' is not used for two and 'both/all' need a plural verb.

gaps.sentence: The hotel was full, so we had to look for ___ hotel.
gaps.explanation: 'Another hotel' means some other, unspecified one; 'the other hotel' would imply exactly two known hotels.

gaps.sentence: ___ the students passed with good grades.
gaps.explanation: Before 'the + noun' use 'most of': 'Most of the students'; 'most the students' is wrong.

gaps.sentence: She was ___ in a bad mood.
gaps.explanation: 'Mostly' is an adverb meaning mainly or usually; 'most' as a quantifier needs a noun.

gaps.sentence: Can I ask you ___ questions about your trip?
gaps.hint: polite request with a countable plural
gaps.explanation: 'A few questions' means some questions and is the natural pattern in polite requests.
